A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, central theorems, algorithms and proof appendices. The text, equations and figures support reliable comparison, including material moved from the introduction to an appendix.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical results, analytical examples and discussions of prior research, but no original experimental or simulation outcomes in the main text or Appendices A–J.

after.justification: Section 11 and Appendix L report original CART simulations, including MSE and feature split-coverage results in Figures 1–6. Section 11 states that results are averaged over 200 replicates.

M1.justification: The central CART, ERM and random-forest procedures remain unchanged. Section 10 newly sketches an extension permitting splits on monomials involving up to k variables, generalizing the preceding discussion of pairwise interactions. This procedural extension is discussed but not implemented in the reported simulations.

E1.justification: v3 introduces the paper's first empirical evaluation coverage: synthetic regression with uniform binary covariates and f(x)=x1*x2+alpha*x1, covering XOR and a weak marginal-signal variant under noiseless and Gaussian-noise scenarios. v1 considers related functions analytically without training or evaluating models on generated datasets.

E2.justification: The new simulations evaluate CART alone. ERM trees, random forests, neural networks, GUIDE and BART remain theoretical or discussion comparisons rather than empirically evaluated baselines. Comparisons between X2 and X3 concern features, not competing methods.

E3.justification: Section 11 adds an empirical protocol varying d over {10,20,30,40,50}, log2(n) over {7,9,11,13,15}, and alpha over {0,0.02}. MSE uses validation-tuned impurity stopping; split coverage uses trees grown to purity. The noisy setting is inconsistent: the setup specifies variance 0.1, whereas Appendix L captions specify 0.01.

E4.justification: New analyses test how dimension, sample size, weak marginal signal and noise affect prediction and feature selection. Figures 2, 4, 5 and 6 compare relevant-feature X2 coverage with irrelevant-feature X3 coverage, directly examining the proposed bottleneck mechanism. v1 has analytical examples but no corresponding empirical sensitivity or mechanism checks.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports averaging simulation results over 200 replicates. v1 has no empirical repeated-run reporting. The addition documents replication but supplies no empirical seed list, standard errors, confidence intervals or error bars.

E6.justification: Figures 1–6 introduce numerical MSE and split-coverage results absent from v1. For example, Figure 1 reports noiseless MSE of 0.86 for alpha=0 and 0.10 for alpha=0.02 at d=50 and n=2^15. These are newly reported outcomes under different regression functions, not a same-setting performance improvement over v1.

T1.justification: The main theorems and proof appendices are retained. Section 7.2 replaces the cited SID rate with an explicit bias–variance derivation; equations (36) and (43) receive mathematical corrections. Old Appendix J, now K, changes the conditional SQ/CSQ-derived sample-complexity assertion from tilde-Theta(d^k) to tilde-Theta(d^(k-1)). Limited complexity reasoning is also added in Section 10 and Appendix A.

C1.justification: The central claims remain the exponential sample requirement for non-MSP greedy trees, logarithmic dimension dependence for generic MSP functions and ERM trees, theoretical comparisons with neural networks, and the coupling proof technique. The simulations support these retained claims without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds an ANOVA/heredity interpretation of MSP, explains that genericity also permits fixed coefficients outside the exceptional set, and qualifies ERM computational hardness by distinguishing fixed from growing dimension. It also interprets the new simulations as evidence for marginal-signal bottlenecks. The principal applicability boundaries remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 11 supplies data-generation instructions, parameter grids and validation-based selection of the impurity threshold for the new simulations. Reproduction remains only partially specified: no implementation version, code access, validation-set size or threshold-search grid is provided, and the stated noise variance conflicts with Appendix L.

R1.justification: v3 adds connections to ANOVA heredity, further coupling precedents, computational-hardness literature and sparse learning under general product measures. Appendix A also corrects the positioning of non-adaptive trees by distinguishing them from honest trees. These additions refine the existing MSP/CART/SGD positioning rather than replacing it.

P1.justification: The title changes from Greedy Recursive Partitioning to Recursive Adaptive Partitioning. The former Section 1.1 moves into an expanded Appendix A, introductory explanations are revised, and simulation sections are added. Most methodological prose and proof organization remain closely matched; there is no extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v1 has no empirical figures; v3 adds six figures containing paired, numerically annotated heatmaps with dimension/sample-size axes and MSE or coverage color scales. Two figures appear in the main text and four in Appendix L, substantially expanding the visual presentation of evidence.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the retained theoretical results more concrete through replicated prediction and feature-selection simulations, improves the explanation and positioning of MSP, and corrects several mathematical statements. These are useful supplementary gains to largely unchanged central guarantees and proofs. The conflicting noise variance and unspecified validation/tuning details limit the reproducibility of the new empirical evidence.
